summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

key_cases.case_name: K.D. v. County of Crow Wing
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment for county and city defendants, the court held that removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permitted only where continued parental custody poses an imminent threat, that officials acting on a reasonable suspicion of abuse have qualified immunity, and that after such a removal the state must promptly initiate judicial proceedings.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the narrow exigency permitting protective custody and the state's duty to seek prompt judicial review afterward.
key_cases.quote: In cases in which continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, emergency removal of children without a court order is constitutionally permitted.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming dismissal of North Dakota parents' § 1983 suit against a social worker and others, the court recognized the parents' substantive due process interest in familial integrity but held that officials pursuing a child-abuse investigation retain qualified immunity when their actions rest on a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the constitutional interest that protective custody intrudes upon in North Dakota's federal circuit.
key_cases.quote: We have long recognized that parents have a liberty interest in familial relationships and have an important substantive due process right to control the care and custody of their children.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois's presumption of unfitness for unwed fathers, while affording a hearing to every other parent, denied him equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: The federal due-process predicate underlying every emergency or protective removal: the State must give the parent a hearing on fitness before permanently depriving him of his children, and cannot substitute a presumption for individualized proof.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that, as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

mandatory_reporters: Listed professionals only — North Dakota is not a universal-reporting state (N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(1))
Tier 1, 2, 3, and 4 mental health professionals (as defined in N.D. Cent. Code § 25-01-01) and any other medical or mental health professional
Religious practitioners of the healing arts
Schoolteachers, school administrators, and school counselors
Child care workers and child care licensors
Juvenile court personnel and probation officers
Licensed social workers and family service specialists
Members of the clergy, except when the knowledge is derived from information received as a spiritual adviser
Any person who discovers images of sexual conduct by a child on a workplace computer (N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(3))
reporting_details: North Dakota is not a universal-reporting state: the professionals listed in N.D. Cent. Code § 50-25.1-03(1) must immediately report orally or in writing to the Department of Health and Human Services or its authorized agent, while any other person may report (N.D. Cent. Code §§ 50-25.1-03(2), 50-25.1-04(1)).

other: A child placed for care or adoption in violation of law

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately if there is a serious threat to the child's life or health; otherwise within department-set time frames

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: An extension of time must be requested of and granted by the department (N.D. Admin. Code § 75-03-19-04).
